newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EMU woes overshadow UK Brown's jobs plan.
newsitem.headline: EMU woes overshadow UK Brown's jobs plan.

text.p: Renewed worries over the progress of European monetary union looked set to overshadow British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's attempt to put employment at the top of the agenda at a meeting of EU finance ministers on Monday.

But Brown stuck firmly to the subject of jobs and refused to be drawn on the problems faced by EU countries as they attempt to meet the tough economic criteria in order to qualify for the single currency.
He said his view -- that employment is the most pressing issue facing Europe -- was winning support.
"I believe I'm getting support for what I am suggesting ought to be the major initiative of Europe on the economy over the next year," he told BBC television in an interview.
That was more important to the European Union than who was going to join in the first round of monetary union in 1999, he said.

"In or out of monetary union, people in Europe now know that unless we face up to the issue of jobs and low growth, Europe will remain sluggish and we will not create the prosperity that everyone wants."
But he said the two were not necessarily incompatible. He told BBC radio it was possible to combine budget discipline with new ways of creating jobs.
Brown prepared the ground for the jobs discussion by circulating a paper to EU finance ministers on Sunday evening.

He said the paper, which follows a letter sent to the ministers last week, laid out three major points for discussion -- job creation and employability, opportunities for small businesses and completing the EU single market.

He said there was support for what the new Labour government was doing in Britain. "There is an echo for what we are doing in Britain...on welfare to work and increasing people's chances of both jobs and job security," he said.

But one finance minister said the paper did not offer any concrete proposals on what EU countries should do to improve their employment prospects. Ruairi Quinn, outgoing finance minister of Ireland, said Brown's paper was "light". "There's not much in it," he told Reuters.
Experts said Brown will probably get his way and a statement will be made on jobs at the end of this one day conference.

"There is a strong commitment to the employment chapter in Europe and, given the build up to this meeting, to not say anything about employment at the end would be a significant ommission," said Graham Bishop, adviser on European econmic affairs at Salomon Brothers in London.
But whatever is agreed on jobs is likely to be eclipsed by talk that European Economic and Monetary Union will not start on time in 1999 due to problems in France and Germany.

A surprise Socialist victory in the French election has raised concerns the new government will not stick to the austerity measures necessary to qualify for EMU. And the shelving of a German government plan to revalue gold reserves to help improve its deficit ratios mean even Europe's powerhouse may struggle to meet the Maastricht criteria.

Finance ministers leaving Sunday's dinner said France seemed as determined as ever to stick to the EMU timetable. But the Financial Times newspaper reported that French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has indicated he will not be rushed into an agreement on EMU at the Amsterdam summit next week.

There are also worries that the new French government will seek to renegotiate the stability pact which will impose fines on govnments whose budget deficits creep up from the Maastricht target once EMU is underway.
Britain's former Conservative government signed up to the pact in Dublin in December, but so far the new Labour government has not said whether or not is will accept its terms.

One of the pact's resolutions states that budget deficits should balance over the course of the business cycle, more restrictive than the British government's 'golden rule' which allows for borrowing to invest over the course of the cycle.
